opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is control. Most of the inpainting tools I've tried are impressive in a demo: you mask out a region, type a prompt, and something plausible appears. But "plausible" isn't the same as "what I wanted." If I'm removing a person from a photo of a street, I want the background to continue in a way that respects the actual geometry of the scene: the vanishing lines, the shadows, the lighting direction, the texture of the pavement. Too often you get something that looks fine at thumbnail size and falls apart when you zoom in, or that hallucinates objects that were never there.

The second thing is consistency. If I'm editing a sequence of images, or a video, or even just making several edits to the same image, the model needs to keep identity and style stable. A face shouldn't subtly change, and the color temperature shouldn't drift between edits. Temporal and semantic coherence is still a weak spot, and it's exactly what matters for real use rather than one-off novelty.

Third is speed and efficiency. Much of my work is about making these models run on devices like phones, not just on big GPU clusters. If an edit takes thirty seconds, or needs a round trip to the cloud, people won't iterate with it the way they do with a normal photo tool. Interactive latency changes how you use something; it becomes a brush rather than a batch job.

Finally, honesty, in a sense. I'd like the tool to know where it's uncertain and to give me options there rather than confidently committing to one answer. Give me a few candidates, let me refine with a stroke or a reference image, and preserve everything outside the mask exactly. When a tool gets those right, being faithful to the scene, being consistent, being fast enough to be interactive, and being controllable, that's when I'd actually trust it in a real workflow.

r001.rationale: The response mentions pavement texture and scene fidelity, but does not identify a mismatch between generated texture and the surrounding image as a practical barrier.

r002.rationale: The response asks that everything outside the mask be preserved, but does not mention visible artifacts along the edited region’s boundary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a good question, because I think a lot of people see the demos and assume the problem is basically solved, and it really isn't once you try to use these things in practice.

The first thing I'd want is consistency. Not just that the filled-in region looks plausible on its own, but that it respects everything around it. The geometry has to line up, the lighting direction has to match, the textures have to continue across the boundary without a seam you notice the moment you zoom in. A lot of models produce something that's locally very convincing but globally wrong, like a wall that doesn't quite meet the floor at the right angle, or a shadow that's falling the wrong way. Humans are extremely sensitive to those cues, even if we can't always articulate what's off.

The second thing is control. If I'm removing an object, I usually have a very specific intent about what should be there instead. I don't want the model to hallucinate a new object into the hole. I want the background to continue in a way that's faithful to the scene. So the tool needs to understand the difference between "fill this with what's plausibly behind it" and "invent something interesting here." And when I do want to guide it, with text or a sketch or a reference, it should actually follow that rather than drifting toward whatever the training distribution favors.

Third, I'd want it to be honest about uncertainty. There are cases where the occluded region is genuinely ambiguous, and a good tool should either give me multiple options or at least not commit confidently to something that could be wrong. In applications like medical imaging or document restoration or anything forensic, confidently fabricating detail is worse than leaving the gap.

And then there's the practical side. It needs to work at full resolution, not just on a downsampled crop that gets upscaled and blurred. It needs to handle video, where the fill has to stay coherent frame to frame, which is much harder than a single image. And it needs to be fast enough that it fits into an interactive workflow, because if I have to wait thirty seconds and then redo it four times, I'll just do it by hand.

So, in short: coherence with the surrounding context, controllability, appropriate humility, and real-world robustness. We've made huge strides on the "looks good in a demo" part. The remaining gap is making it trustworthy enough that you don't feel you have to check every pixel afterward.

r001.rationale: It says the filled textures should continue across the boundary and describes locally convincing results that are globally wrong, identifying mismatch with the surrounding image.

r002.rationale: It identifies a noticeable seam at the boundary as a problem, describing it as something visible when zooming in.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key is control. If I want to remove an object or fill in a missing region, the tool needs to understand the surrounding image—the geometry, the lighting, the texture—and produce something consistent with it. A result can look realistic on its own and still be wrong for that particular scene.

And it should preserve the parts I didn’t ask it to change. If I have to inspect the entire image after every edit, that limits how useful it is. I’d want an interactive process where I can guide the result, correct it easily, and get predictable behavior. Producing an impressive example is one thing; doing the edit I intended reliably is what would make me use it.

r001.rationale: The response says the tool must match the surrounding image’s texture and produce a consistent result, identifying inconsistency as a practical problem.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention visible artifacts or issues along the edited region’s boundary.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the first thing is consistency. You can generate a region that looks very realistic by itself, but does it belong in that image? Does the lighting match? Is the perspective correct? If you are filling in part of a person or an object, does the structure make sense?

Then there is control. There may be many plausible ways to fill a missing region, and the tool’s first choice may not be what I want. I need a way to guide it and refine the result without changing the parts of the image I wanted to preserve. So it’s not just producing something visually impressive. It’s producing something that fits my intention, reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a generated region fits the image, including lighting and perspective, but does not identify a texture mismatch with the surrounding image.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention visible artifacts along the edited region’s boundary.
